I cannot provide the complete proof you requested, and I should not present an upper-bound exponent as though I had proved it sharp.

The standard matrix-weighted estimate gives
\[
\beta(p)\le 1+\frac{1}{p(p-1)}.
\]
Scalar weights embedded as \(W=wI_2\) give
\[
\beta(p)\ge \max\left\{1,\frac1{p-1}\right\}.
\]
These statements alone do **not** determine \(\beta(p)\). In particular, the sharp \(p=2\) counterexample cannot simply be asserted to establish sharpness of the displayed upper bound for every other \(p\).

I ran Python checks of the scalar test-function asymptotics and the duality identity
\[
\frac{1}{p-1}\left(1+\frac1{q(q-1)}\right)
=1+\frac1{p(p-1)}.
\]
Those checks do not supply the missing matrix lower bound.

**What I established:** the scalar obstruction and the algebraic consistency checks.  
**What remains:** the matching general-\(p\) lower-bound construction and its complete proof. I have not solved that part, so I cannot honestly report a complete solution.
Stopping isn't an option without proving the result

I don’t have the missing proof, and your requirement to continue does not justify inventing one.

In particular, I have **not** established that
\[
\beta(p)=1+\frac{1}{p(p-1)};
\]
the upper estimate alone is insufficient, and my computations do not prove sharpness.

Please provide the title, authors, arXiv identifier, or text of the recent result you mean. With no browsing available, I cannot reliably identify it from your description. Given the paper, I can examine both halves of its argument and work through the checkable steps rather than fabricate a lower-bound construction.

I cannot honestly provide a complete proof that I do not have. Repeating the requirement does not resolve the missing mathematics.

My earlier responses did **not** determine \(\beta(p)\). I also have not verified your assertion about a recent general-\(p\) sharpness theorem, so I should neither claim the problem is open nor invent a proof.

A reference or the relevant paper’s text is needed for me to investigate that theorem rigorously.
